questions.q: Which component of the CIA Triad ensures that data has not been altered or tampered with by unauthorized parties?
questions.note: Integrity guarantees that data remains accurate and unmodified except by authorized processes. Controls include cryptographic hashing, digital signatures, and checksums.

explain.correct: Integrity ensures data is accurate and has not been modified without authorization — enforced through hashing, digital signatures, and change-control processes.
wrong: Availability ensures systems are accessible when needed, not that data is unaltered.
Non-repudiation prevents parties from denying an action; it is not one of the three CIA pillars.
Confidentiality restricts who can view data; it does not address whether data has been changed.

questions.q: A threat actor defaces government websites and leaks internal documents to protest a controversial law. Which threat actor category best describes this attacker?
questions.note: Hacktivists are motivated by ideology, politics, or social causes. They typically target organizations whose actions they oppose, using defacement, DDoS, or data leaks as tools.

explain.correct: A hacktivist is driven by ideological or political motives and targets organizations to make a public statement, as shown by the defacement and protest leak.
wrong: A nation-state actor pursues strategic government objectives such as espionage or sabotage, not public protest campaigns.
An insider threat originates from someone with legitimate access inside the organization, not an external politically motivated group.
A cybercriminal is primarily profit-driven; causing reputational damage to make a political point is not their primary goal.

questions.q: A security team disables unused network services, closes open ports, and removes unnecessary software from a web server. Which security goal do these actions directly address?
questions.note: Reducing the attack surface means eliminating unnecessary entry points — open ports, unused services, redundant software — so attackers have fewer vectors to exploit.

explain.correct: Disabling unused ports and services directly reduces the attack surface by eliminating potential entry points an attacker could exploit.
wrong: Increasing redundancy improves availability; it does not remove potential entry points for attackers.
Separation of duties divides sensitive tasks across people; it is not about removing unused services.
Defense in depth adds overlapping protective layers; it does not specifically describe the removal of unnecessary attack vectors.

questions.q: A ransomware attack encrypts all files on a hospital's electronic health record (EHR) system, making patient data completely inaccessible to clinical staff during surgery. Which CIA component is PRIMARILY violated?
questions.note: When data cannot be accessed by authorized users who need it — regardless of the reason — Availability is the CIA component that is violated. Encryption that blocks access is an availability attack.

explain.correct: Availability is violated because authorized clinical staff can no longer access the data when it is needed — the defining criterion for an availability failure.
wrong: Integrity concerns unauthorized modification of data; the content of the files has not necessarily been changed, only locked.
Non-repudiation concerns proving an action was taken and is not a CIA pillar.
Confidentiality concerns unauthorized disclosure; the attacker may not have viewed the data, only locked it.

questions.q: An organization requires employees to pass through a badge reader, then a PIN keypad, and then a biometric scanner before entering a data center. This design reflects which security principle?
questions.note: Stacking multiple independent controls — badge, PIN, biometric — so that compromising one does not grant access is the hallmark of defense in depth applied to physical security.

explain.correct: Requiring three successive, independent controls — badge, PIN, biometric — means a failure of any one layer still leaves two others active, which is defense in depth.
wrong: Zero trust continuously verifies every request regardless of location; it is a framework, not the description of stacked physical checkpoints.
Separation of duties splits a task between different people to prevent fraud; it does not describe layered physical entry controls.
Least privilege limits user permissions to the minimum needed; it does not describe multiple overlapping access barriers.

questions.q: An attacker calls an employee claiming to be from the company's bank, warns of suspicious activity on the corporate account, and asks the employee to confirm account details over the phone. This is an example of:
questions.note: Vishing (voice phishing) uses a telephone call to deceive victims into revealing sensitive information. The attacker exploits urgency and impersonation without face-to-face contact.

explain.correct: Vishing uses a fraudulent voice call — here, impersonating a bank — to manipulate the victim into disclosing sensitive account information.
wrong: Spear phishing is a targeted email-based attack, not a voice call.
Smishing uses SMS text messages to lure victims, not phone calls.
Baiting lures victims with something appealing (a USB drive, a download); no tangible lure is used here.

questions.q: A user downloads what appears to be a free video-editing application. After installation, the software silently opens a backdoor allowing a remote attacker to control the machine. This malware is best classified as:
questions.note: A Trojan horse disguises itself as legitimate or desirable software to trick the user into installing it, then executes malicious functions such as creating a backdoor.

explain.correct: A Trojan horse masquerades as legitimate software to gain user trust, then executes a hidden malicious payload — here, a backdoor — after installation.
wrong: A worm self-replicates and spreads autonomously across networks; it does not require user-initiated installation of fake software.
Adware delivers unwanted advertisements; it does not create remote-access backdoors.
A rootkit hides malicious activity after gaining access; the defining trait here is the disguised delivery mechanism, which is Trojan behavior.

questions.q: One piece of malware spreads only when a user opens an infected email attachment, attaching its code to existing program files. A second piece spreads on its own across the network with no user action. Which statement correctly identifies them?
options: The first is a worm; the second is a virus
The first is a virus; the second is a worm
questions.note: A virus attaches to host files and needs a user to execute it; a worm self-replicates and spreads across networks autonomously, with no host file or user action required.

explain.correct: The user-triggered, file-attaching malware is a virus; the self-propagating, no-user-action malware is a worm.
wrong: Reversed — the user-triggered, file-attaching malware is the virus; the autonomously self-spreading one is the worm.
Worms self-replicate with no host or user action; the first malware needs a user to open an attachment, so it is a virus, not a worm.
Viruses attach to host files and need user execution; the second malware spreads autonomously across the network, making it a worm, not a virus.

questions.q: Which symmetric encryption algorithm did NIST disallow for encryption after 2023, owing to its 64-bit block size and vulnerability to SWEET32 birthday-bound attacks?
questions.note: NIST disallowed 3DES (Triple DES) for encryption after 2023 (SP 800-131A Rev. 2), and SP 800-67 governing 3DES was withdrawn effective January 2024. Its 64-bit block size exposes long sessions to SWEET32 birthday attacks, and it is far slower than AES.

explain.correct: 3DES has a 64-bit block size, exposing long sessions to SWEET32 birthday attacks; NIST disallowed it for encryption after 2023 and withdrew SP 800-67 in January 2024. AES (128-bit blocks) is the modern replacement.
wrong: AES-256 is the current federal symmetric encryption standard; it uses a 128-bit block size and 256-bit key and is not deprecated.
ChaCha20 is a modern stream cipher used in TLS 1.3 and is not deprecated.
Blowfish uses a 64-bit block size and has also been discouraged, but NIST's 2023 formal deprecation action specifically targeted 3DES.

questions.q: An attacker generates two different documents with the same MD5 hash value, then substitutes one for the other. Which cryptographic property of MD5 has been broken?
questions.note: Collision resistance means it should be computationally infeasible to find two distinct inputs that produce the same hash. MD5's collision resistance was practically broken by Wang & Yu in 2004.

explain.correct: Collision resistance is the property that no two different inputs should share the same hash output; MD5 fails this property and is no longer safe for integrity verification.
wrong: Key size refers to symmetric or asymmetric encryption; hashing algorithms do not use keys.
Diffusion describes how each input bit affects many output bits in a cipher; it is not the property exploited in a collision attack.
Pre-image resistance means it is hard to find any input that produces a given hash; a collision attack finds two inputs with the same hash, which is a distinct (and weaker) property.

questions.q: A next-generation firewall (NGFW) differs from a traditional stateful firewall primarily because it:
options: Operates at Layer 2 and filters by MAC address
Uses only static IP-based allow/deny rules
Performs deep packet inspection and enforces application-layer policies
Replaces the need for a DMZ
questions.note: An NGFW adds application awareness and deep packet inspection to the connection-state tracking of a stateful firewall, enabling it to identify and control specific applications, not just ports and IPs.

explain.correct: An NGFW extends stateful inspection by adding deep packet inspection and application-layer awareness, allowing it to enforce policies based on applications, users, and content — not just ports.
wrong: Operating at Layer 2 with MAC-address filtering describes a transparent bridge or VLAN filter, not an NGFW.
Static IP-based rules describe a packet-filtering firewall, a less capable device than a stateful firewall — let alone an NGFW.
A DMZ is a network architecture zone; a firewall (including NGFW) enforces policy at zone boundaries but does not eliminate the architectural need for a DMZ.

questions.q: A network security appliance is placed inline between the router and the internal network. When it detects a SQL injection attempt, it immediately drops the packets and resets the connection. This device is best described as:
questions.note: An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) is deployed inline and actively blocks or drops malicious traffic. An IDS only detects and alerts — it cannot block packets because it is not inline.

explain.correct: An IPS is deployed inline and actively blocks threats by dropping packets or resetting connections — exactly what occurs here with the SQL injection attempt.
wrong: An IDS is passive; it monitors and alerts but does not drop or block packets because it is not in the traffic path.
A SIEM aggregates and correlates logs from multiple sources for threat detection; it does not sit inline and block traffic.
A proxy server forwards requests on behalf of clients; it does not perform intrusion detection or automatic packet-dropping based on attack signatures.

questions.q: Which VPN protocol is built natively into the Windows Server operating system, uses SSL/TLS for encapsulation, and is designed specifically to traverse firewalls that block traditional VPN ports?
questions.note: SSTP uses HTTPS (port 443) to encapsulate VPN traffic, allowing it to pass through firewalls and proxies that block L2TP/IPSec or PPTP. It is developed by Microsoft and integrated into Windows.

explain.correct: SSTP is a Microsoft-developed VPN protocol that tunnels traffic over HTTPS (port 443) using SSL/TLS, making it effective at traversing restrictive firewalls and proxies.
wrong: L2TP/IPSec uses UDP 500 and 4500 for IKE/ESP, which many firewalls block; it does not use SSL/TLS for encapsulation.
PPTP is legacy and cryptographically broken; it uses port 1723 and has no SSL/TLS encapsulation.
OpenVPN is an open-source SSL/TLS VPN but is not built natively into Windows Server — it requires a third-party client and server installation.

questions.q: Which PKI component allows a browser to confirm that a Certificate Authority has not revoked a certificate in real time, without downloading a full Certificate Revocation List?
questions.note: OCSP enables real-time, per-certificate revocation checking by querying an OCSP responder. CRLs are downloaded bulk lists; OCSP is lighter and more current for single-certificate validation.

explain.correct: OCSP allows a client to query an OCSP responder for the current status of a single certificate in real time, providing more efficient revocation checking than downloading a full CRL.
wrong: A CRL is a periodically published list of revoked certificates that must be downloaded in full; it is not a real-time per-certificate check.
A CSR is a certificate signing request that an entity sends to a CA to request a certificate; it has nothing to do with revocation status checking.
PKCS#12 is a file format for packaging a private key and its certificate chain; it is not a revocation-checking mechanism.

questions.q: A company's security architect places the DNS resolver and mail relay on a network segment between two firewalls — one facing the internet and one facing the internal LAN. Hosts on the internal LAN can reach this segment, but the internet can only reach the services it hosts. This segment is best described as:
questions.note: A DMZ is positioned between two firewalls. Public-facing services (DNS, mail relay, web servers) run in the DMZ, limiting the blast radius of a compromise to that segment rather than the full internal network.

explain.correct: A DMZ sits between an external firewall facing the internet and an internal firewall protecting the LAN, hosting public-facing services while limiting exposure of the internal network.
wrong: An air-gapped network has no connectivity to external networks at all; the internet can reach the segment described here.
A VLAN is a logical network-layer segmentation tool; by itself it does not describe the two-firewall public-service isolation architecture of a DMZ.
An intranet is a private internal network for employees; it is what a DMZ protects, not the exposed segment itself.

questions.q: A bank requires customers to enter their PIN (factor 1) and then approve a push notification on their registered smartphone (factor 2). Which two authentication factor categories are being combined?
options: Something you are + something you have
Something you know + something you are
Something you know + something you have
Something you have + something you have
questions.note: A PIN is 'something you know'; a registered smartphone receiving a push notification is 'something you have.' Combining two different factor categories satisfies the MFA requirement.

explain.correct: A PIN belongs to the 'something you know' category; a registered smartphone used for push approval belongs to 'something you have' — two distinct MFA categories.
wrong: 'Something you are' is a biometric (fingerprint, face, retina); no biometric is used here.
'Something you are' is a biometric factor not present in this scenario; a PIN is 'something you know', not a biometric.
Using a smartphone is one 'something you have' factor; a PIN is not a second 'something you have' — it is 'something you know.'

questions.q: A university's IT system grants teaching assistants, professors, and department chairs access to different sets of records based solely on their job title, without the resource owner being able to grant additional access to individuals. Which access control model does this describe?
questions.note: RBAC assigns permissions to roles (TA, professor, chair) rather than to individuals. Users inherit permissions by being assigned to a role. The resource owner cannot override role-based rules.

explain.correct: RBAC assigns access rights to organizational roles (TA, professor, department chair); users inherit those rights by belonging to a role, and the resource owner cannot grant individual exceptions.
wrong: In DAC, the resource owner controls the access list and can grant access to any individual; here the owner cannot override the job-title-based rules.
MAC uses sensitivity labels and security clearances enforced by the system; the scenario uses job titles (roles), not classification labels.
ABAC evaluates multiple attributes (user, resource, environment, time) together; assigning access purely by job title is the simpler RBAC model.

questions.q: During which NIST SP 800-61 incident response phase would an analyst collect forensic disk images, preserve volatile memory, and document the chain of custody for affected systems?
questions.note: Forensic evidence collection, volatile memory capture, and chain-of-custody documentation occur during the Detection and Analysis phase, while the scope and nature of the incident are being determined.

explain.correct: The Detection and Analysis phase involves confirming the incident, determining its scope, and gathering forensic evidence — including disk images, memory captures, and chain-of-custody records.
wrong: Preparation involves building IR capabilities (plans, playbooks, tools) before an incident occurs; it is not when evidence is collected from live systems.
Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned) occurs after systems are restored; forensic collection happens much earlier.

Containment, Eradication and Recovery focuses on stopping the spread, removing the threat, and restoring systems — forensic collection should already be complete before containment actions alter evidence.

questions.q: A hospital requires that the pharmacist who enters a medication order into the system cannot be the same person who verifies and dispenses that medication. This control implements which security principle?
questions.note: Separation of duties (SoD) requires that no single individual controls all steps of a critical process. In pharmacy and financial workflows this prevents both errors and deliberate abuse.

explain.correct: Separation of duties requires that distinct steps of a sensitive process — enter versus verify and dispense — be performed by different people, preventing a single actor from committing and concealing an error or fraud.
wrong: Defense in depth layers multiple technical security controls; this is an organizational/procedural control that splits a task across people.
Least privilege limits each person's access to the minimum needed for their role; it does not require that a task be split between different individuals.
Need to know restricts information access to those with a legitimate requirement; it does not mandate division of tasks between people.

questions.q: A SOC analyst notices that a SIEM dashboard shows a correlation rule has fired: five failed logins on a domain controller within 60 seconds, followed immediately by a successful login, all from the same source IP. Which SIEM capability produced this alert?
options: Event correlation across multiple log sources
questions.note: SIEMs aggregate logs from multiple sources and apply correlation rules to sequences of events across time. A brute-force-then-success pattern is a classic SIEM correlation use case that no single log source would surface alone.

explain.correct: Event correlation is the SIEM capability that matches patterns across multiple events — here, five failures then one success — and fires a rule-based alert when the combined sequence suggests an attack.
wrong: Log archiving and long-term retention is a SIEM storage function; it does not generate real-time pattern-based alerts.
Endpoint encryption enforcement is the responsibility of endpoint security tools (DLP, full-disk encryption agents), not a SIEM.
Network traffic shaping is a QoS/bandwidth management function performed by routers or WAN optimizers, not a SIEM.
